### Problem: Reverse Pairs {#sec-salgo-p2-c}

::: {.p-statement}

Given an integer array `nums` ($1 \le n \le 5 \cdot 10^4$, $-2^{31} \le \mathit{nums}[i] \le 2^{31}-1$), return the number of **reverse pairs**: indices $(i, j)$ with $i < j$ and $\mathit{nums}[i] > 2 \cdot \mathit{nums}[j]$.

Source: [LC 493 · Reverse Pairs](https://leetcode.com/problems/reverse-pairs/){.solved difficulty="Hard"}

Example — `nums = [1, 3, 2, 3, 1]`. Output `2` — the pairs $(1,4)$ and $(3,4)$, both with $\mathit{nums}[\cdot]=3 > 2\cdot 1$.
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
This is the inversion count of @sec-salgo-p2-a with one twist: the predicate is not "greater" but "more than twice". Every pair is either inside one half (counted recursively) or crosses the midpoint, and the crossings can still be counted in linear time **because both halves are already sorted**: the "$> 2\times$" relation between two sorted halves is a monotone two-pointer sweep. What changes is that this sweep is no longer the merge's own comparison, so it becomes a separate pass just before the merge.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **All-pairs scan.** Test every $i < j$ against `nums[i] > 2*nums[j]`. $O(n^2)$, exact — the oracle.
2. **Merge sort with a cross count.** Recursively sort both halves; before merging, walk the sorted left run with an index $j$ into the sorted right run that only ever advances: for each left value, all right values still satisfying $> 2\times$ form a growing prefix. Add its length, then do the ordinary stable merge. $O(n \log n)$.

**Invariant.** After each recursive call its slice is sorted and holds exactly the input multiset, so the cross count sees two sorted runs and the monotone $j$ never misses or double-counts a crossing pair.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### All-pairs scan

::: {.form-next}
For each ordered pair $i < j$, check the $> 2\times$ predicate. $O(n^2)$ time, $O(1)$ extra — the definition and the checker for the fast form. Beware overflow: $2 \cdot \mathit{nums}[j]$ can leave the int range, so widen before doubling.

**Worked example.** $[1,3,2,3,1]$: only $3 > 2\cdot 1$ fires, at positions $(1,4)$ and $(3,4)$ → total 2.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("revpair", "brute")
    assert str(final) == "2"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def rp493_brute(nums):
    return sum(1 for i in range(len(nums)) for j in range(i + 1, len(nums))
               if nums[i] > 2 * nums[j])
```

##### C++

```cpp
// all-pairs scan, O(n^2) oracle; widen before doubling
long long rp493Brute(const vector<int>& nums) {
    long long cnt = 0;
    int n = (int)nums.size();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; ++j)
            if ((long long)nums[i] > 2LL * nums[j]) ++cnt;
    return cnt;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** Python's arbitrary-precision integers make `2 * nums[j]` safe here, but C++ must cast to `long long` first: with $\mathit{nums}[j]$ near $2^{31}$ the doubled value overflows a 32-bit int. The $O(n^2)$ loop is exactly what the $n = 5 \cdot 10^4$ limit forbids, so the merge form is not a luxury.

#### Merge sort with a cross count

::: {.form-next}
Sort-and-count in one recursion. Split at the midpoint; count reverse pairs inside each half recursively. Then count **crossing** pairs: with the two halves sorted, a pointer $j$ into the right half advances (never retreats) as left values grow, so the crossings are tallied in $O(n)$. Finally merge the two sorted runs. $O(n \log n)$ total.

**Worked example.** Split at the midpoint: $[1,3]\mid[2,3,1]$. The right half $[2,3,1]$ hides one reverse pair on its own ($3>2\cdot1$, the pair $(3,4)$), and recursing leaves the two runs sorted as $[1,3]$ and $[1,2,3]$. Now count crossings: left $1$ beats no right value ($1>2\cdot1$ fails); left $3$ beats right $1$ ($3>2\cdot1$, the pair $(1,4)$) but not right $2$ ($3>4$ fails). One crossing $+$ one inside the right half → total $2$.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("revpair", "merge")
    assert str(final) == "2"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-salgo-493-merge
def rp493_merge(nums):
    a = list(nums)

    def sort_count(lo, hi):
        if hi - lo <= 1:
            return 0
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        cnt = sort_count(lo, mid) + sort_count(mid, hi)
        j = mid
        for i in range(lo, mid):
            while j < hi and a[i] > 2 * a[j]:
                j += 1
            cnt += j - mid
        out, i, k = [], lo, mid                # then the ordinary stable merge
        while i < mid and k < hi:
            if a[i] <= a[k]:
                out.append(a[i]); i += 1
            else:
                out.append(a[k]); k += 1
        out.extend(a[i:mid]); out.extend(a[k:hi])
        a[lo:hi] = out
        return cnt

    return sort_count(0, len(a))

for _ in range(300):
    x = [random.randint(-40, 40) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 30))]
    assert rp493_merge(x) == rp493_brute(x)
big = [2**31 - 1, -2**31, 2**30, -(2**30) - 1, 1, -1]  # extreme values: 2 * x leaves the int range
assert rp493_merge(big) == rp493_brute(big)
assert rp493_merge([1, 3, 2, 3, 1]) == 2
assert rp493_merge([2, 4, 3, 5, 1]) == 3
assert rp493_merge([-5, -5]) == 1
print("rp493_merge OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
// merge sort counting crossings, O(n log n); watch the doubling overflow
long long rp493SortCount(vector<long long>& a, vector<long long>& buf, int lo, int hi) {
    if (hi - lo <= 1) return 0;
    int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
    long long cnt = rp493SortCount(a, buf, lo, mid) + rp493SortCount(a, buf, mid, hi);
    int j = mid;
    for (int i = lo; i < mid; ++i) {
        while (j < hi && a[i] > 2LL * a[j]) ++j;
        cnt += j - mid;
    }
    merge(a.begin() + lo, a.begin() + mid, a.begin() + mid, a.begin() + hi, buf.begin() + lo);
    copy(buf.begin() + lo, buf.begin() + hi, a.begin() + lo);
    return cnt;
}
int reversePairs(vector<int>& nums) {
    vector<long long> a(nums.begin(), nums.end()), buf(nums.size());   // widen once, up front
    return (int)rp493SortCount(a, buf, 0, (int)a.size());
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** The cross count reuses the sortedness the recursion just produced. Both runs are ascending, so as the left pointer $i$ advances to a *larger* value, every right value that already satisfied `a[i] > 2*a[j]` still does: the qualifying prefix of the right run only grows. That is why $j$ never rewinds; across all $i$ it advances at most `hi - mid` times, so the tally is linear, and the merge that follows is the stable merge of @sec-salgo-a3 (`std::merge` in C++). The count is a separate pass because the merge compares `a[i]` with `a[k]`, not with `2 * a[k]`, so the two pointers do not move together. Converting to `long long` once, before the recursion, removes the overflow for good.
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**All-pairs** is $O(n^2)$ time, $O(1)$ space. **Merge counting** is $O(n \log n)$ time, $O(n)$ space. The skeleton is identical to @sec-salgo-p2-b — same divide, same "the halves are sorted so crossings are linear" trick — which is the point of pairing them.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- Overflow is the trap: `2 * nums[j]` must be computed in 64-bit, for negative values as much as positive ones ($2 \cdot (-2^{31})$ is below the 32-bit range). Python integers do not overflow, so the Python test can only check the logic on extreme values; the C++ widens to `long long` before doubling.
- $n \le 1$ → 0 pairs. All equal zeros → 0 (need strictly $> 2\times$).
:::

- [CF 911D · Inversion Counting](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/911/D){rating="1800"} — count inversions once, then track only their parity under segment reversals.
